derives_from: This table starts from `hi__hi-IN.json`'s phoneme inventory and abugida slot-spelling engine -- both are a property of Devanagari, not of Hindi, so reusing them is the same move Persian's `Arab` stack reuse is. No published Marathi respelling-key standard was found (unlike Hindi's Bhargava/Rapidex pair, or Spanish's DPD): Marathi dictionaries such as Molesworth's give meanings, not a foreign-sound-to-Devanagari correspondence table, and no Marathi-language-authority pronunciation-hint convention turned up during this pass. So this table's *contents* are inherited from Hindi's, which was itself built on Bhargava's page layout and Rapidex's letter choices, and its three *departures* are Marathi's own grammar, named and argued in `deviations` below. Anywhere this disagrees with a real Marathi respelling convention this pass did not find, that is the place to fix first.

deviations.rule: ɭ -> ल (Hindi's own choice, since Hindi has no ळ)
deviations.why: Overruled: ɭ -> ळ instead. Marathi has ळ natively -- बाळ, आळस, गोळा -- so a target's retroflex lateral (Tamil ள், IPA /ɭ/) gets the letter that actually is the sound, rather than the merger with plain /l/ that Hindi's own vocabulary forces it into. Checked against the shipped `deva*.ttf` faces (already carry ळ, used throughout `data/lang/mr/*.csv`), so no font question.

deviations.rule: the syllable_fixup stripping a word-final halant (`'match': '्([,;:.!?]*)$', 'out': '\1'`)
deviations.why: Dropped outright. Hindi's word-final schwa deletion is categorical and lexicalised -- every fluent reader already knows which real Hindi words end bare, which is what lets Hindi's table rely on it. A respelling is by definition a sequence no reader has seen before and must sound out mechanically, and Marathi's school-taught reading convention for an unfamiliar bare consonant -- unlike Hindi's -- does not default to silence: Marathi's schwa deletion is real but far less categorical than Hindi's well-documented syncope (the two are regularly cited as differing on exactly this point), so a bare final consonant in a *novel* string is the one place relying on it is least safe. Probed directly: the `mr` espeak voice itself reads a real Marathi word's medial schwa inconsistently against its final one (`कमळ` -> `kˈʌməɭ`, keeping the medial अ and dropping the final one) -- i.e. even native vocabulary does not follow one simple rule, so a table that assumed Hindi's rule for foreign spellings would be guessing. Keeping the halant is the same treatment every interior conjunct already gets in both tables; nothing new was added, an existing rule was simply not overruled at the word edge.

deviations.rule: /ts/ -> त्स and /dz/ -> ज़ against plain च/ज (Hindi's own choice)
deviations.why: Kept, after considering and rejecting the tempting alternative. Marathi's own च/ज genuinely alternate between [tʃ]/[dʒ] and [ts]/[dz] depending on the *following vowel* (front vowel -> palatal, back/central -> dental) -- but that is Marathi's own conditioning, not the source word's, and the engine's phoneme rules are slot-based (onset/coda/any) rather than aware of the following nucleus across a rule boundary. Reusing plain च for a source /ts/ would come out right only when the source's own following vowel happened to match Marathi's rule and wrong otherwise (German `Zeit`, English `tsunami`), and a `syllable_fixups` regex correcting that would have to avoid every one of the many unrelated च/ज instances /tʃ/ and /dʒ/ already emit -- a large surface for a cosmetic gain (त्स reads as a heavier cluster than a bare च, nothing more is at stake). The unconditionally correct spelling was kept instead -- the same call RESPELL-SYSTEMS.md records for Persian's `q1` -> `q`: prefer the repair that adds no new risk.

deviations.rule: policy.reader_onsets, policy.max_onset and the whole `approximations` block (Hindi's own measurements)
deviations.why: Inherited without independent verification against a Marathi corpus of comparable size to Hindi's -- both languages are Indo-Aryan with broadly similar consonant-cluster tolerance, so this is a reasonable starting point rather than a measured Marathi result. Flagged here rather than silently reused: a fluent Marathi speaker re-running the measurement Hindi's own note describes (`--units`, cluster-count comparison against a reviewed sheet) is the next step this table has not taken.

approximations: Sounds with no Devanagari letter, and what they get. /ʔ/ and /ʕ/ are written as nothing, which is what Hindi already does with Arabic hamza and ain (अरब, इस्लाम) and which leaves a Thai zero onset correctly bare. /ħ/ is ह. /θ ð/ are थ द, following Rapidex (थैंक्स, देन) and Hindi's own habit; they collide with /t̪ d/ for the dental targets, which is the documented cost. /x ɣ q/ are ख ग क. /ç/ is ख where the target has an /x/ for it to be the front allophone of (German ich -> इख, München -> म्यूनिख) and ह where it does not (Japanese ひ -> ही). /y yː ʉ/ are यू and /ɵ/ is यो, which is Hindi's own reading of a front rounded vowel (म्यूनिख, ज़्यूरिख, यूरो, मिन्यू); /ø œ/ are ओ (कोलोन, गोएथे). /ɯ/ is उ, following the romanisation its two largest holders use -- Japanese u and Korean ㅡ -- at the cost of Turkish ı. /ɤ/ is ए, which is what Hindi print gives Mandarin's e (देगुओ, हेनान). /ɲ/ is न्य and /ʎ/ ल्य. Vietnamese's glottalised codas and its /ˀ/ are dropped with the tone they belong to. Retroflex /ʂ ʈʂ ʈʂʰ/ merge into श च छ, since ष is read [ʃ] by Hindi speakers and would spell a distinction nobody pronounces. Korean's /ɰ/ and Mandarin's /ɥ/ are व and य.
note:
**Devanagari's abugida structure and the virama-placement logic are inherited unchanged from `hi__hi-IN.json`** -- see that table's own note for the full argument (bare-vs-virama-vs-matra by slot, the inherent-vowel-visibility test, the nine structural invariants `--units`-style checks confirm). Nothing about that machinery is Hindi-specific; it is a fact about Devanagari.

**What is Marathi-specific is the three deviations above, and this table's own measurements below**, run the same way Hindi's were.

Legend: '’' marks the syllable to stress, exactly where Bhargava places it and for the same typographic reason Hindi's table gives -- U+02B9 has no glyph in either shipped Devanagari face, so U+2019 stands in, already inside the subsetter's Latin range and colliding with nothing Devanagari writes.
